summary.text: Separating the factors divisible by \(p\) in the relevant factorial ratios reduces the problem to products over units modulo \(p^r\); pairing \(j\) with \(p^r-j\) and expanding these products through cubic order turns the required valuations into cancellations of inverse-power sums over the units. The resulting product congruences and the base approximations \(\binom{2p^L}{p^L}\equiv2\), \(\binom{3p^L}{p^L}\equiv3\) are combined by an algebraic identity, with the one-power loss at \(p=3\) compensated by an extra factor of \(3\) in the correction term.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
All products and divisibility statements below are over the integers unless a residue ring is explicitly mentioned.

For an integer \(s\ge1\), put
\[
U_s=\{j:1\le j\le p^s,\ p\nmid j\}.
\]
(The endpoint \(p^s\) is harmless because it is excluded by \(p\nmid j\).) Define
\[
D_s=\prod_{j\in U_s}j,
\qquad
B_{m,s}=\prod_{j\in U_s}(mp^s+j).
\]
We shall need several facts about these products.

### 1. Pairing the factors

The map \(j\mapsto p^s-j\) permutes \(U_s\). Indeed, if \(1\le j<p^s\) and \(p\nmid j\), then \(1\le p^s-j<p^s\), and \(p\nmid p^s-j\). Consequently,
\[
D_s^2=\prod_{j\in U_s}j(p^s-j).
\]
More generally, pairing one copy of \(B_{m,s}\) using this permutation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{m,s}^{2}
&=\prod_{j\in U_s}(mp^s+j)\bigl(mp^s+(p^s-j)\bigr)\\
&=\prod_{j\in U_s}\left(j(p^s-j)+m(m+1)p^{2s}\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, if
\[
c_j=j(p^s-j),
\]
then \(D_s^2=\prod c_j\) and \(B_{m,s}^2=\prod(c_j+m(m+1)p^{2s})\).

We will use the elementary product expansion
\[
\prod_{j\in U_s}(c_j+x)
\equiv \prod_{j\in U_s}c_j+xE_{1,s}\pmod{x^2},
\tag{2}
\]
where
\[
E_{1,s}=\sum_{i\in U_s}\prod_{\substack{j\in U_s\\j\ne i}}c_j.
\]
This follows simply by expanding the product: the constant term is \(\prod c_j\), the terms containing exactly one \(x\) have total \(xE_{1,s}\), and every remaining term contains at least two copies of \(x\).

We also need the expansion through degree two. Define the ordered second elementary sum
\[
E_{2,s}=\sum_{i\in U_s}\ \sum_{\substack{k\in U_s\\k\ne i}}
\prod_{\substack{j\in U_s\\j\ne i,k}}c_j.
\]
Since every unordered pair occurs twice in \(E_{2,s}\), direct expansion gives
\[
2\prod_{j\in U_s}(c_j+x)
\equiv 2\prod_{j\in U_s}c_j+2xE_{1,s}+x^2E_{2,s}
\pmod{x^3}.
\tag{3}
\]

### 2. Divisibility of the harmonic product sums

We first determine enough divisibility of \(E_{1,s}\).

Suppose first that \(p\ge5\). Work modulo \(p^s\). Every \(j\in U_s\) is a unit, and
\[
c_j=j(p^s-j)\equiv-j^2\pmod{p^s}.
\]
Writing \(P=\prod_{j\in U_s}c_j\), we may divide each omitted-factor product by \(c_i\), obtaining
\[
E_{1,s}\equiv P\sum_{i\in U_s}c_i^{-1}
=-P\sum_{i\in U_s}i^{-2}\pmod{p^s}.
\tag{4}
\]
The elements of \(U_s\), reduced modulo \(p^s\), are exactly the units of \(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z\). Inversion permutes these units, so
\[
\sum_{i\in U_s}i^{-2}=\sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^\times}u^2.
\]
Call this latter sum \(S\). Multiplication by \(2\) also permutes the units, and hence
\[
S=\sum_u(2u)^2=4S.
\]
Thus \(3S=0\) modulo \(p^s\). Since \(p\ge5\), the residue class of \(3\) is invertible, so \(S=0\). Equation (4) therefore gives
\[
p^s\mid E_{1,s}\qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{5}
\]

For \(p=3\), the same argument still yields \(3S=0\), although one can no longer cancel \(3\) modulo \(3^s\). It follows from (4) that
\[
3^s\mid 3E_{1,s},
\]
and cancellation in the integers gives
\[
3^{s-1}\mid E_{1,s}.
\tag{6}
\]

Next, for every prime \(p\) and every \(s\ge2\), we claim
\[
p\mid E_{2,s}.
\tag{7}
\]
To see this, reduce modulo \(p\). Again \(c_j\equiv-j^2\), and all the \(c_j\)'s are units. For any finite family of units one has
\[
E_2=\left(\prod_jc_j\right)
\left(\left(\sum_jc_j^{-1}\right)^2-\sum_jc_j^{-2}\right).
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, after factoring out \(\prod c_j\), the right side is the sum of \(c_i^{-1}c_k^{-1}\) over all ordered pairs \(i\ne k\), which is exactly the definition of \(E_2\).

Now each nonzero residue class modulo \(p\) occurs exactly \(p^{s-1}\) times among the members of \(U_s\). Since \(s\ge2\), this multiplicity is divisible by \(p\). Therefore, modulo \(p\), the sum over \(U_s\) of any function depending only on the residue class is zero. In particular,
\[
\sum_{j\in U_s}c_j^{-1}=0,
\qquad
\sum_{j\in U_s}c_j^{-2}=0
\pmod p.
\]
Equation (8) proves (7).

### 3. A valuation lemma for \(B_{m,s}-D_s\)

We record a general consequence of (1), (2), and the preceding harmonic divisibility. Suppose
\[
p^e\mid E_{1,s},\qquad p^f\mid m(m+1),
\qquad e\le 2s+f.
\tag{9}
\]
Then
\[
p^{2s+e+f}\mid B_{m,s}-D_s.
\tag{10}
\]

Set \(x=m(m+1)p^{2s}\). From (1), (2), and \(D_s^2=\prod c_j\),
\[
B_{m,s}^2-D_s^2=xE_{1,s}+R,
\qquad x^2\mid R.
\]
The first term is divisible by \(p^{2s+e+f}\). The remainder is divisible by \(p^{4s+2f}\), and the inequality in (9) says
\[
2s+e+f\le4s+2f,
\]
so the remainder has the required divisibility as well. Thus
\[
p^{2s+e+f}\mid B_{m,s}^2-D_s^2
=(B_{m,s}-D_s)(B_{m,s}+D_s).
\]
But modulo \(p\), \(B_{m,s}\equiv D_s\), while \(p\nmid D_s\). Hence
\[
B_{m,s}+D_s\equiv2D_s\not\equiv0\pmod p,
\]
because \(p\ge3\). Thus \(B_{m,s}+D_s\) is relatively prime to every power of \(p\), and cancellation proves (10).

Two cases of (10) will be used later, both with \(m=1\):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
p\ge5:&p^{3s}\mid B_{1,s}-D_s,\\[2mm]
p=3:&3^{3s-1}\mid B_{1,s}-D_s.
\end{array}
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed, for \(p\ge5\) take \(e=s,f=0\) and use (5); for \(p=3\) take \(e=s-1,f=0\) and use (6).

### 4. A weighted product congruence

Define
\[
A_{2,s}=B_{1,s}=\prod_{j\in U_s}(p^s+j),
\qquad
A_{3,s}=B_{2,s}=\prod_{j\in U_s}(2p^s+j).
\]
We claim that for \(s\ge2\),
\[
p^{3s+3}\mid A_{3,s}^2-3A_{2,s}^2+2D_s^2.
\tag{12}
\]

Let \(t=p^s\), \(c_j=j(t-j)\), and put
\[
Q_x=\prod_{j\in U_s}(c_j+x).
\]
The pairing identity (1) gives
\[
D_s^2=Q_0,
\qquad A_{2,s}^2=Q_{2t^2},
\qquad A_{3,s}^2=Q_{6t^2}.
\tag{13}
\]
Apply the cubic expansion (3), first with \(x=2t^2\), then with \(x=6t^2\). Taking the second congruence minus three times the first makes both the constant and linear terms cancel in precisely the combination in (12). Equivalently, for some integer \(K\),
\[
Q_{6t^2}-3Q_{2t^2}+2Q_0
=12t^4E_{2,s}+12t^6K.
\tag{14}
\]
By (7), the first term on the right is divisible by \(p^{4s+1}\), and the second by \(p^{6s}\). Since \(s\ge2\),
\[
3s+3\le4s+1,
\qquad
3s+3\le6s.
\]
Thus both terms in (14) are divisible by \(p^{3s+3}\). Together with (13), this proves (12).

### 5. The product ratio identity for binomial coefficients

For \(s\ge1\) and \(m\ge0\), one has
\[
D_s\binom{(m+1)p^s}{p^s}
=B_{m,s}\binom{(m+1)p^{s-1}}{p^{s-1}}.
\tag{15}
\]
Here is a direct derivation. In the product of the integers from \(1\) to \(pN\), separate the factors divisible by \(p\) from those not divisible by \(p\):
\[
(pN)!=\left(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le pN\\p\nmid i}}i\right)p^N N!.
\]
Likewise, in the product
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{pN}(pM+i)=(pN)!\binom{pM+pN}{pN},
\]
the factors with \(p\mid i\) contribute
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{N}(pM+pk)
=p^N\prod_{k=1}^{N}(M+k)
=p^NN!\binom{M+N}{N}.
\]
Canceling the positive common factor \(p^NN!\), and then taking
\(M=mp^{s-1}\), \(N=p^{s-1}\), yields (15).

Combining (15) with the valuation lemma gives useful congruences for binomial coefficients. Let
\[
C_{m,s}=\binom{(m+1)p^s}{p^s}.
\]
Equation (15) says
\[
D_s(C_{m,s}-C_{m,s-1})=(B_{m,s}-D_s)C_{m,s-1}.
\tag{16}
\]
Since \(p\nmid D_s\), any power of \(p\) dividing \(B_{m,s}-D_s\) also divides \(C_{m,s}-C_{m,s-1}\).

For \(p\ge5\), (5) and the valuation lemma show, for \(m=1,2\), that
\[
p^{3s}\mid C_{m,s}-C_{m,s-1}.
\]
In particular every step is divisible by \(p^3\). Telescoping from level \(0\), where \(C_{m,0}=m+1\), gives for every \(L\ge0\)
\[
\binom{2p^L}{p^L}\equiv2\pmod{p^3},
\qquad
\binom{3p^L}{p^L}\equiv3\pmod{p^3}.
\tag{17}
\]

For \(p=3\), (6) gives slightly different strengths. With \(m=1\), the valuation lemma gives
\[
3^{3s-1}\mid C_{1,s}-C_{1,s-1},
\]
which is always at least divisibility by \(3^2\). Hence
\[
\binom{2\cdot3^L}{3^L}\equiv2\pmod{3^2}.
\tag{18}
\]
With \(m=2\), there is an additional factor of \(3\) in \(m(m+1)=6\). Thus in (9) we may take \(e=s-1\) and \(f=1\), obtaining
\[
3^{3s}\mid C_{2,s}-C_{2,s-1}.
\]
Telescoping gives
\[
\binom{3\cdot3^L}{3^L}\equiv3\pmod{3^3}.
\tag{19}
\]

### 6. Final algebraic assembly

Fix now \(r\ge2\), and abbreviate
\[
D=D_r,
\quad A_2=A_{2,r},
\quad A_3=A_{3,r},
\]
\[
\beta_2=\binom{2p^r}{p^r},
\quad \beta_3=\binom{3p^r}{p^r},
\quad b_2=\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}},
\quad b_3=\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}.
\]
The ratio identity (15), with \(m=1\) and \(m=2\), says
\[
D\beta_2=A_2b_2,
\qquad
D\beta_3=A_3b_3.
\tag{20}
\]
Also, (12) says
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid A_3^2-3A_2^2+2D^2.
\tag{21}
\]

Set
\[
\Delta=\beta_3^2-27\beta_2-b_3^2+27b_2.
\]
Using (20), a direct algebraic expansion gives the key identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
D^2\Delta={}&b_3^2(A_3^2-3A_2^2+2D^2)\\
&+3b_3^2(A_2-D)^2\\
&+3D(2b_3^2-9b_2)(A_2-D).
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
For completeness, this can be checked by replacing \(D\beta_3\) by \(A_3b_3\) and \(D\beta_2\) by \(A_2b_2\) on the left, then expanding the two squares and collecting terms.

We now estimate the three terms on the right of (22).

#### Case 1: \(p\ge5\)

By (11),
\[
p^{3r}\mid A_2-D.
\tag{23}
\]
At level \(L=r-1\), (17) gives
\[
p^3\mid b_3-3,
\qquad p^3\mid b_2-2.
\]
The identity
\[
2b_3^2-9b_2=2(b_3-3)(b_3+3)-9(b_2-2)
\]
therefore yields
\[
p^3\mid2b_3^2-9b_2.
\tag{24}
\]
The first term on the right of (22) is divisible by \(p^{3r+3}\) by (21). The second is divisible by \(p^{6r}\) by (23), and \(6r\ge3r+3\) because \(r\ge2\). The third is divisible by \(p^{3r+3}\) by (23) and (24). Hence
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid D^2\Delta.
\]
Since none of the factors in \(D\) is divisible by \(p\), \(D^2\) is relatively prime to \(p^{3r+3}\), and consequently
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid\Delta.
\tag{25}
\]

#### Case 2: \(p=3\)

Now (11) gives
\[
3^{3r-1}\mid A_2-D.
\tag{26}
\]
At level \(L=r-1\), (18) and (19) say
\[
9\mid b_2-2,
\qquad27\mid b_3-3.
\]
Write
\[
b_2=2+9y,
\qquad b_3=3+27x.
\]
Then
\[
2b_3^2-9b_2
=81(18x^2+4x-y),
\]
so
\[
3^4\mid2b_3^2-9b_2.
\tag{27}
\]
Again the first term in (22) has the required divisibility by (21). The second is divisible by \(3^{2(3r-1)}\), and
\[
2(3r-1)\ge3r+3
\]
for \(r\ge2\). The third is divisible, by (26) and (27), by
\[
3^{(3r-1)+4}=3^{3r+3}.
\]
Thus \(3^{3r+3}\mid D^2\Delta\). Since \(3\nmid D\), cancellation again gives (25).

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta
&=\left(\binom{3p^r}{p^r}^{2}-27\binom{2p^r}{p^r}\right)
 -\left(\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}^{2}-27\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}\right)\\
&=a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore (25) is exactly
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}},
\]
as required.
